The wedding was celebrated at the Peak Church on Thursday, December 24, of Mr. Harold Walter Hewett (son of the late Mr. H. C. Hewett of North Shields, Northumberland, and the late Mrs. D. Urquhart) and Miss Evelyn Lennox Paterson (daughter of Captain and the late Mrs. Paterson, of Ilford, Essex). The Rev. T. B. Powell, M.A., officiated.
The function was of a very quiet nature, only relatives and a few intimate friends being present.

With a bouquet of pink roses and orange blossoms, the bride was dressed in a charming gown of silver-grey French silk with hat and shoes to match. She was given away by Mr. James Smith. Mr. A. Urquhart was the "best man."

Leaving the church the party proceeded to No. 12, "Conduit Road (residence of Mr. J. Smith) where the reception was held. The honeymoon is being spent at Repulse Bay. The bride's travelling dress was of beige crepe-dechine, trimmed with fur, and she wore a nigger-brown georgette hat.
This afternoon St. John's Cathedral was the scene of a pretty wedding.

The contracting parties were Mr. Shiu-pun Preston (second son of Mr. and Mrs. Wong Yu-ning of 74, Peel Street) and Miss Phyllis Grace Jan See Chin (eldest daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Jan See Chin of Hau Tau, Heungshan, and formerly of Cairns, North Queensland, Australia).
The service was conducted by the Rev. A. D. Stewart, M.A., assisted by the Cathedral Chaplain, the Rev. T. B. Powell, M.A. Mr. F. Mason, A.R.C.O., L.T.C.L., was at the organ.

The bride's dress was of white brocade charmeuse, trimmed with white charmeuse: She wore an embroidered tulle veil and her shoes were of silver brocade. Her bouquet was of white roses set off with maiden hair fern and matched with white ribbon.

Miss Norma (sister of the bride) acted as bridesmaid. She was dressed in blue crepe-de-chine with silver lace trimming and hat to match. Her bouquet was of pink and white roses, set off with maiden-hair fern and matched with pink ribbon.
The Misses Irene and Dorothy (also sisters of the bride) were flower-girls. They were both attired in pale pink satin with hats to match.
The bride's mother wore a dress of navy crepe-de-chine, trimmed with silver vieux rose, and hat to match.
Mr. Jan See Chin gave his daughter away and Mr. Tso Tsun-on acted as "best man."
After the wedding service a reception was held at the King Edward Hotel.
The honeymoon is being spent at the Shatin Gap Bungalow. The bride's travelling dress was of navy serge with oriental embroidery, with hat to match.
A Chinese seaman pleaded guilty at the Central Magistracy this morning to a charge of unlawful possession of dutiable liquor.

The charge was in respect of two bottles of Martell's brandy which the defendant brought ashore when he landed from a sampan at the Praya near the Western Market yesterday afternoon. On being accosted by a revenue officer, defendant dropped the package on the road, one of the bottles being broken.
A fine of $10 was imposed and order was made for the liquor to be confiscated.

A NEW TURN IN THE NEGOTIATIONS.

Friendly discussions have taken place in the last few days with the result that the terms of settlement of the Hongkong-Canton situation have been greatly simplified. A delegation of Hongkong Chinese merchants will shortly join with the Canton Chinese merchants in negotiations with the Strike Committee for the cessation of the boycott.
Evidence was taken at the Central Magistracy this morning in the case against two Russian women who are charged with alleged theft of four rolls of satin, valued at $475, from the Wing On Company.
Mr. C. A. S. Russ appeared to the defence.

A salesman giving evidence stated that he suspected some rolls of cloth were missing from a show case during a visit paid by the defendants on Tuesday afternoon. Seeing one of the defendants holding her overcoat tightly when walking away from the counter, witness followed them. One of the defendants then drew a roll of satin from under her overcoat and laid it on the table. Following the other defendant to the verandah, witness said that three other rolls were seen to be protruding from under the coat.

Cross-examined by Mr. Russ, witness denied the suggestion that the defendants took the cloth near a window to examine it. He also denied that he lost his temper and quarrelled with them. (Case proceeding).

News of the appointment of the Hon. Mr. A. G. M. Fletcher, Acting Colonial Secretary of Hongkong, as Colonial Secretary of Ceylon has been received by his many friends with genuine pleasure and the Colony of Hongkong joins in its appreciation of a well-merited promotion. The Hon. Mr. Fletcher well deserves the honour, being a most conscientious and able officer to whose energy and judgment successive Governors have paid tribute.

In addition to his official duties in the Colony, which extend over nearly a quarter of a century, Mr. Fletcher has specialised in a question of great concern to Crown Colonies like Hongkong which derive a large part of their revenue from the licensed traffic—that of opium suppression. He was Hongkong's representative on the League of Nations Opium Commission at Geneva and his able speeches there demonstrated the insight he had into all aspects of the problem.

A well-merited honour was conferred on Mr. Fletcher in June, 1922, when the King was pleased to approve his appointment as Companion of the Most Distinguished Order of St. Michael and St. George. Mr. Fletcher had three years previously appeared in the Honours List when he was created a Commander of the Order of the British Empire.
Mr. Fletcher first came to the Colony in 1902 during which year he acted as British Consul at Macao, whilst in the following year he was seconded for famine relief work in Kwangsi. In addition to numerous Government posts he was Secretary to the Military Service Commission, Chairman of the Vital Requirements and Shipping Control Committee and Clerk to the General Military Service Commission.
Mr. Fletcher, in his new post, will succeed H.E. the Governor of Tongkong (the Hon. Mr. Cecil Clementi, C.M.G.) who came from Caylon where he had been for some years. Colonial Secretary of Mr. and Mrs. Fletcher have Hongkong next Saturday.
The alertness of two Chinese detectives early on Xmas morning led to the prevention of what might have been an extensive robbery at the premises of Wm. Powell, Ltd.

Recent robberies (generally on Saturday nights or at holiday times when the robbers have had time to make extensive preparations) led the police to have extra patrols on the look out this holiday week-end. Two of the detectives (Insp. Chu Heung and P.C. Lu Muk) on the Des Vaux Road patrol made an examination of the private alley way between the Bank of East Asia and the buildings of Powell's.

Flashing their torches (this was at 3 a.m.) they saw a man sitting in a ricsha pretending to sleep. Whilst talking to him they again flashed their torches up the alley way and saw a shadow moving. Taking the man already under arrest with them, the detectives walked to the blind end and found a man lying on the flag stones, also feigning to sleep. By his side was a basket to all outward appearances containing paper. When this was searched it was found to contain a pair of pliers, an electric torch and some
When searched, the second man was found to have a knife in his possession. Neither had a cent on them.

Charged at the Central Magistracy, the second man said he was ill and was sleeping. The Magistrate remarked that he chose a peculiar place for a sick man to lie down. Prisoner was sentenced to, two months' imprisonment for loitering with intent to commit a felony and four months for being in possession of house breaking implements.
The man first arrested, who the police stated 'was undoubtedly keeping guard whilst the other should attempt to effect entry, was sentenced to two months hard labour.
Sub-Insp. Fallon was in charge of the police case.
A Chinese woman who enticed a man from Chinese into British territory where he was arrested for murder was cross-examined this morning by prisoner's counsel.
She denied that the man had come willingly. She had only got him to come on the pretext of signing property deeds. He told her that he had violated Hong-kong's laws and was afraid of being arrested.

Witness also denied the suggestion of Mr. Elsley Zeitlyn (instructed by Mr. G. K. Hall Brutton, for the prisoner) that the prisoner had been badly beaten and kicked in the course of the struggle which took place just inside the British border to which she had brought prisoner.
Witness contradicted herself on certain points and when confronted with former statements said that she was confused by “counsel's loud voice.” She was not used to being shouted at, she stated.

Cross-examination of this witness having finished, that of other police witnesses was given in chief. When the Crown case closes, there will be seven witnesses for the defence and the case will not conclude, it is thought, until Wednesday or Thursday.

kong Hotel, beautifully decorated
for the occasion, was the scene of
much gaiety on Boxing Day even-

by the management was held. It
was attended by four hundred
and fifty revellers who, thanks to
the excellence of the arrangements
for their comfort and to
the carnival spirit manifest in
each and all, were able to bring the
day to a happy and fitting con-
clusion.

The diffused rays from the hanging lamps, played upon the fancy costumed throng and an excellent band-discoursed music. Squeakers and streamers were everywhere in evidence and an excellent band-discoursed music. It was a tired but happy gathering which broke up at 1 a.m., many members with the avowed intention of renewing acquaintance on the occasion of the New Year's Carnival to be held at the Repulse Bay Hotel next Thursday evening when fancy or evening dress will again be optional. Special arrangements for conveyance to the Peak and the City are to be made.
An overflow dance is arranged to take place at the Hotel Grill Room.

Defending an elderly Chinese passenger by the s.s. "President Jefferson" who was charged at the Kowloon—Magistracy this morning with unlawfully having in his possession a portion of a revolver, Mr. J. T. Prior said that the defendant while in America had heard of the armed robberies committed in China and brought the weapon with him for his own protection.

Stealing a motor cycle belonging to Mr. P. Vickers while he was on a visit at a friend's house at Cameron Road, Kowloon, on Xmas Day, a Chinese left the machine by way of security for a meal he had taken at a restaurant. No sooner had the machine been restored to its owner by the efforts of the Police than it was spirited away again the following morning from outside Cambay Buildings. Trying the same dodge at another restaurant, the thief was caught.
These facts were given in evidence when the man was charged at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning on four charges of theft and obtaining meals with intent to defraud.
Defendant, who pleaded guilty to the latter charges, was sentenced to four months hard labour altogether.

The Congress of the National Labour Secretariat presided over by the Dutch Communist, Mr. Sneevliet, and attended by representatives of the British Minority Party, also by the Soviet, adopted a resolution by 118 votes to 4, instructing the Executive to give effect to the resolution adopted by the referendum of 1923 to join the Red Trade Union International. It also adopted a resolution by 118 votes to 3, in favour of the Red Trade Union International issuing invitations to the World Congress of Red Trade Union International, and to the International Federation of Trade Unions and organisations not belonging to both internationalis.
The death has occurred of Surgeon-Admiral John Cassillis Birkmyre Maclean, who was responsible for the naval transport service in war time.

[A son of the Rev. A. Maclean, D.D., Surgeon-Admiral Maclean was educated at Aberdeen University and entered the Navy in 1872, from which he retired in 1907. He was present at the bombardment of Alexandria and in the Egyptian Campaign, 1882, when he was specially promoted. He was born on August 28, 1849.]
